submission.natural_language_explanation: This pole is a retrospective register/topic detector for prose about people as social and political actors: it is driven by the surrounding passage's social-and-public-affairs vocabulary (racism, feminism, immigration, multiculturalism, minorities, protests, journalism, extremism, parliament, court, university, Islam), and it sits at exactly zero on description of physical, chemical, engineering or everyday-object subject matter (combustion, corrosion, hydraulics, alloys, enzymes, reactors, pipes, weather) even in identical sentence frames. It is context- and passage-sensitive rather than a detector of any fixed token set - token identity explains only 31% of its variance, the same sentence raises it when the clause is about society and drops it to zero when the subject is swapped for a technical one - and it additionally spikes, more weakly and content-independently, on the paragraph-break newline token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Retrospectives of the suffrage campaign usually begin with the great processions and end with the ballot, but the minute books that survive from the regional branches tell a slower and more awkward story. In the mill towns of the north, the organisers spent more years arguing with one another than with the government. One branch came within a single vote of splitting in 1907 over whether married women should be admitted on the same terms as men, and the quarrel was patched over only when a wealthy manufacturer agreed to guarantee the rent on the meeting hall for another two years.

The correspondence is full of the same complaints. Speakers cancelled at short notice. Collections came in short because the factory hands had already given to the strike fund. The secretary of the Bradford society wrote to the national office in March 1909 asking whether it was permissible to hold a meeting in a public house, and received a reply three weeks later saying that it was not, but that no one would be sent to check. Historians who have read the whole run of letters, rather than the published pamphlet, tend to conclude that the movement was held together less by doctrine than by the sheer administrative persistence of a few dozen women who could type.

That reading has consequences for how the eventual enfranchisement is explained. If the branches were as divided as the records suggest, then the claim that a single national leadership steered the campaign to victory becomes difficult to sustain, and the pressure that finally moved the House of Commons looks less like a moral argument won in public and more like a coalition assembled ward by ward. The petitions were signed in kitchens and at factory gates, and the men who carried them into the chamber were answering a constituency organisation that had been built over fifteen years.

What the retrospective view also changes is the ending. The ballot was extended to some women in 1918 and to all of them a decade later, but the societies did not dissolve; they turned to housing, to the wages of shop workers, to the feeding of schoolchildren, and to the question of whether a woman could be admitted to the bar. The same network of committees, the same subscription lists, the same people who had once sold newspapers on street corners were now drafting evidence for select committees and briefing members before a debate. Seen from the branch records, the vote was less an ending than a transfer of the organisation's attention, and the political history of the following twenty years is difficult to read without it.
